questions.q: Which kind of writing is primarily writer-centred?
questions.explain: They are written for the benefit of the writer; workplace writing should be reader-centred.
questions.evidence: Things like diaries and journals are primarily writer-centred, in that they are written for the benefit of the writer.

questions.q: What does reader-centred writing advise you to emphasise?
options: What you can do rather than what you can't
questions.explain: Focus on the positive.
questions.evidence: Focus on the positive: emphasize what you can do rather than what you can’t.

questions.q: Which question should you ask yourself before writing for a reader?
options: How long can I make this?
How many big words can I use?
Which font is the most decorative?
questions.explain: Audience analysis starts with knowing who will read it.
questions.evidence: Use these guidelines and ask yourself the following questions: Who is my target audience?

questions.q: What is the first step in designing any solution?
questions.explain: Design processes vary, but they start with the problem.
questions.evidence: One commonality you will likely find in examining other people’s design process diagrams is this: the first step in designing any solution is to clearly define the problem .

questions.q: What are many workplace communication tasks designed to do?
options: Solve a problem or improve a situation
questions.explain: That is why writing can follow a design process.
questions.evidence: In the workplace, many of the communications tasks you perform are designed to solve a problem or improve a situation.

questions.q: What question defines a "rhetorical situation"?
options: How many pages should it be?
Who is talking to whom about what, how, and why?
questions.explain: Its five components are purpose, writer, audience, message and context/culture.
questions.evidence: To define a “rhetorical situation,” ask yourself this question: “who is talking to whom about what, how, and why?”

questions.q: In the rhetorical situation, what does PURPOSE refer to?
questions.explain: Determining purpose is part of task analysis.
questions.evidence: PURPOSE refers to the why you are writing.

questions.q: What should you do if your document introduces many new terms?
options: Collect the definitions into a glossary
Use different words for each term each time
Put them all in the title
questions.explain: Define new terms, or link to existing explanations.
questions.evidence: If your document is introducing many terms, collect the definitions into a glossary.

questions.q: If a good explanation of an unfamiliar term already exists, what should you do?
options: Copy it word for word without credit
questions.explain: Don't reinvent the wheel.
questions.evidence: If the term already exists, link to a good existing explanation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson compare changing a term midway to renaming a variable in code?
options: Because writers should learn to code
Using terms consistently matters, just as code won't compile with inconsistent names
questions.explain: Use terms consistently.
questions.evidence: Use terms consistently If you change the name of a variable midway through a method, your code won’t compile.

questions.q: Which voice should the vast majority of sentences in technical writing use?
questions.explain: Active voice is usually clearer.
questions.evidence: The vast majority of sentences in technical writing should be in active voice.

questions.q: What is the formula of an active-voice sentence?
questions.explain: A passive sentence reverses the formula.
questions.evidence: Active Voice Sentence = actor + verb + target A passive voice sentence reverses the formula.

questions.q: According to many technical writers, what is the most important part of a sentence?
questions.explain: Pick the right verb and the rest will follow.
questions.evidence: Choose strong verbs Many technical writers believe that the verb is the most important part of a sentence.

questions.q: What is wrong with sentences that start with "There is" or "There are"?
options: They marry a generic noun to a generic verb
questions.explain: Often you can delete "There is" and use the true subject.
questions.evidence: Reduce there is / there are Sentences that start with There is or There are marry a generic noun to a generic verb.

questions.q: What do technical writers aim for, compared with comedy and horror writers?
questions.explain: Clarity is the technical writer's goal.
questions.evidence: Clear sentences Comedy writers seek the funniest results, horror writers strive for the scariest, and technical writers aim for the clearest.

questions.q: What makes a heading effective?
options: Concrete, descriptive language that tells the reader what to expect
questions.explain: Descriptive headings help readers navigate.
questions.evidence: Effective headings use concrete, descriptive language to tell the reader what to expect from the content of each section.

questions.q: What kind of headings should you avoid in technical reports?
options: "Function" headings that name a section's function instead of its content
questions.explain: Readers find content-describing headings more helpful.
questions.evidence: Avoid “function” headings when writing technical reports.

questions.q: When should you use a numbered list instead of a bulleted list?
options: Only for items with numbers in them
questions.explain: Rearranging a numbered list changes its meaning.
questions.evidence: Use a bulleted list for unordered items; use a numbered list for ordered items.

questions.q: What is an embedded (run-in) list?
options: A list inside a table cell
A list whose items are stuffed within a sentence
questions.explain: Long embedded lists are often clearer as bulleted or numbered lists.
questions.evidence: An embedded list (sometimes called a run-in list) contains items stuffed within a sentence.

questions.q: What happens if you rearrange the items in a bulleted list?
options: The list's meaning does not change
questions.explain: Bullets are for unordered items.
questions.evidence: In other words: If you rearrange the items in a bulleted list, the list's meaning does not change.

questions.q: Which is the most important sentence of any paragraph?
questions.explain: Busy readers focus on opening sentences.
questions.evidence: Write a great opening sentence The opening sentence is the most important sentence of any paragraph.

questions.q: What do good opening sentences establish?
options: A joke to warm up readers
questions.explain: Focus your writing energy on opening sentences.
questions.evidence: Good opening sentences establish the paragraph's central point.

questions.q: What is "netiquette"?
options: Proper etiquette for using the internet
questions.explain: Professional texting, email and social media require it.
questions.evidence: Text messaging, emailing, and posting on social media in a professional context requires that you be familiar with “netiquette,” or proper etiquette for using the internet.

questions.q: Why should a business email have a clear, brief, specific subject line?
options: It helps the recipient understand the essence of the message
It hides the email from spam filters
questions.explain: The subject line previews the message.
questions.evidence: Include a clear, brief, and specific subject line: this helps the recipient understand the essence of the message.

questions.q: What should your written business communication be?
options: Long, formal and full of jargon
As short as possible, even if unclear
questions.explain: It represents you and your company.
questions.evidence: your goal is to make it clear, concise, constructive, and professional.

questions.q: What are letters, in business communication?
options: Brief messages often sent to recipients outside the organisation
questions.explain: They are often on letterhead and limited to one or two pages.
questions.evidence: Letters are brief messages sent to recipients that are often outside the organization.

questions.q: What is a proposal, in the technical sense?
options: A summary of last year's sales
A document that tries to persuade the reader to implement a plan or approve a project
questions.explain: Proposals are persuasive documents.
questions.evidence: A proposal, in the technical sense, is a document that tries to persuade the reader to implement a proposed plan or approve a proposed project.

questions.q: What are proposals often written in response to?
questions.explain: RFPs come from government agencies, organisations or companies.
questions.evidence: Proposals are often written in response to a Request For Proposals (RFP) by a government agency, organization, or company.

questions.q: What does a progress report do?
options: Assures the reader the project is on time and on budget, or explains why not
questions.explain: Like proposals, progress reports are persuasive.
questions.evidence: progress reports assure the reader that the project is on time and on budget, or explain rationally why things might not be going according to the initial plan.

questions.q: Which special notices do instructions use to alert readers to risks?
options: Note, warning, caution and danger notices
questions.explain: They warn about ruined equipment, failed procedures or injury.
questions.evidence: For these situations, you use special notices —note, warning, caution, and danger notices.

questions.q: What are instructions, as described in the lesson?
options: Step-by-step explanations of how to assemble, operate, repair or maintain something
questions.explain: They are one of the most common uses of technical writing.
questions.evidence: One of the most common and important uses of technical writing is to provide instructions, those step-by-step explanations of how to assemble, operate, repair, or do routine maintenance on something.

questions.q: What voice and tone does the Google style guide recommend?
options: Conversational, friendly and respectful, without slang
questions.explain: Sound like a knowledgeable friend.
questions.evidence: In your documents, aim for a voice and tone that's conversational, friendly, and respectful without using slang or being overly colloquial or frivolous.

questions.q: Who should your writing sound like, according to the style guide?
options: A knowledgeable friend who understands what the reader wants to do
questions.explain: Use a casual, natural, approachable voice.
questions.evidence: Try to sound like a knowledgeable friend who understands what the developer wants to do.

questions.q: How many people have an accessibility need, according to the World Health Organization estimate quoted?
options: About 15% of the world's population, more than 1 billion people
questions.explain: Accessible writing improves the experience for everyone.
questions.evidence: The World Health Organization estimates that 15% of the world's population (more than 1 billion people) have an accessibility need.

questions.q: Which tool does the guide suggest using to test your documentation's accessibility?
questions.explain: Testing with assistive technology reveals problems.
questions.evidence: Use a screen reader to test your documentation.

questions.q: Why use descriptive headings and titles?
options: They help readers navigate the browser and the page
They hide content from search engines
They are required by law in every country
questions.explain: Unique headings make jumping between sections easier.
questions.evidence: Use descriptive headings and titles because they help a reader navigate their browser and the page.

questions.q: What is internationalization?
options: Designing a product and its documentation to minimise the localisation effort
Using as many idioms as possible
questions.explain: For example, keeping all UI strings in a separate file.
questions.evidence: Internationalization: Designing a product and its associated documentation to minimize the localization effort—for example, placing all UI strings in a separate file to simplify translation.

questions.q: What does localisation involve besides translation?
options: Adapting things like local currencies and units of measurement
questions.explain: Localisation is more than translating words.
questions.evidence: This process involves more than translation—for example, using local currencies or units of measurement.

questions.q: What should you do if a sentence's meaning is still ambiguous?
questions.explain: Clear, unambiguous language helps global readers.
questions.evidence: If the meaning is still ambiguous, try rephrasing the sentence.
